result:
If I get to choose, I want to write about windows at dusk.

Not grand windows. Not stained glass or floor-to-ceiling glass in magazine apartments. I mean ordinary windows, just after the light has gone blue, when people inside have switched their lamps on but haven't yet drawn the curtains.

From a train, from a street, from the opposite side of a small courtyard, you get them for half a second each. A whole life, framed.

One window: a kitchen, yellow as butter, somebody standing at the sink with their sleeves pushed up, talking over their shoulder to someone you can't see.

Another: completely empty except for a houseplant so large and determined it seems to be running the apartment now. A fern with ambitions.

Another: blue television light flickering on a ceiling. Somebody is watching a football game, or a nature documentary, or falling asleep to the news. You will never know which.

I love how little they give you, and how much your brain refuses to accept that as enough.

Because we don't just *see* a window. We furnish it. We give the person at the sink a name and a long day and a joke they're about to finish telling. We decide the plant-owner waters it on Sundays and talks to it while the kettle boils. We invent anniversaries and arguments and grocery lists stuck to fridges just out of view. Give a human being a lit rectangle and three silhouettes, and they will write you a novel by Tuesday.

We do this everywhere, of course. Not just with windows. With the couple laughing too loudly at the next table. With an old man carefully folding a newspaper on a park bench. With a stranger crying, very quietly and politely, on the bus, as if apologizing for having weather inside her. We catch one line of dialogue — *“Well, I told Margaret not to bring the dog”* — and suddenly we know Margaret. We have opinions about Margaret. We hope, vaguely, that the dog is okay.

It's a kind of trespassing, but a gentle one. And maybe an essential one.

Because most of life is exactly this: partial views. We never get the whole house. Not with strangers, not with friends, not even with the people we have loved for twenty years and watched grow older across a kitchen table. There is always a room we haven't been in. A year they don't talk about. A thought that arrives at 3 a.m. and leaves before morning without leaving a note.

And yet we live together anyway. We guess, we fill in, we get it wrong, we correct ourselves when the curtain opens a little wider. *Oh, I thought you were angry. I was just tired. Oh, I thought you didn't care. I didn't know how to say I did.*

I think that's why those dusk windows feel so tender rather than lonely. They aren't saying, *look how separate we all are* — though we are, in our lit boxes, stacked in rows up the sides of buildings. They're saying, *look how much life is happening that has nothing to do with you, and isn't that wonderful?*

Somewhere right now, in a window you will never pass, someone is learning to play an instrument badly and persistently. Someone is burning toast and laughing about it. Someone is dancing in socks while they wait for pasta water to boil. Someone is reading the last page of a book very slowly because they don't want it to end. Someone is sitting in the dark they haven't bothered to turn a lamp on against, thinking about whether to call their brother.

None of it needs an audience to count.

If I'm allowed to wander, I always end up here: I like unfinished glimpses because they teach the imagination manners. They remind you not to mistake the part you can see for the whole story. To hold your theories lightly. To be curious instead of certain.

Hold the curtain open just a fraction longer. Then let it fall.

The train moves on. Another window, another kitchen, another plant plotting world domination. The night gets properly dark. And for a second, the world feels both impossibly large and impossibly close, like a city full of lit rooms, each one briefly, beautifully yours to imagine, and none of them yours to keep.
